A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cognitive deficits are common among opioid substitution treated patients and that they are not necessarily related to opioid dependence but rather to the treatment and/or the substance abuse.
buprenorphin treatment does not improve attention and memory in opioid-dependent patients, but may improve some aspects of executive functioning.
buprenorphined patients have less cognitive impairment than methadone patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cognitive functioning in opioid-dependent individuals treated with bupernorphine, methandone, or other medications is impaired, and that cognitive functioning in buprenophine patients may improve during treatment.
buprenorphines' superiority over methadone in cognitive performance is not as robust as has been claimed.
buprenorphines cognitive advantage over methadone is small and may disappear when patients with comorbid psychiatric or substance abuse problems are included in the study.
